activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Grayson found his teddy bear on the floor. "Teddy is cold," said Grayson. He wrapped teddy in a soft sock blanket. He patted teddy's tummy, pat, pat, pat. Teddy's eyes went quiet and still. "Look, Mommy! My patting made teddy sleepy."

Mommy smiled. "You have magic hands." Grayson put on his red boot, just one boot, like a daddy at work. He stomped around the room. Stomp, stomp, stomp.

Then he held up a wooden spoon like a wand. "I will do a spell," he said. He tapped the empty box three times. "Wake up, box!" The box became a baby's bed. Grayson laid teddy inside.

"Is teddy alone in there?" asked Mommy.

"No," said Grayson. "Bunny sleeps here too." He tucked bunny in next to teddy. Then he hummed a little song. Both toys lay still and cozy under the sock blanket.

"Shh," whispered Grayson. He stomped his boot away on tiptoe.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Gabriel sat at the kitchen table. Mom gave him a big pink pencil. "Now you can write your name!" she said.

Gabriel squeezed the pencil in his whole fist. He pushed down hard. The pencil point ripped right through the paper. "Oh no!" said Gabriel. There was a big hole where the G should be.

Mom turned the paper over. "Try again," she said. She showed him how to pinch the pencil near the tip. Gabriel held it with just his fingers. He made a round, round G. Then a little a. Then a b. The letters went across the page in a wobbly line.

A woman came to the door. It was Grandma! "What is this?" she asked. Gabriel held up the paper.

"That says Gabriel," he said. "I wrote it all by myself." Grandma clapped her hands.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Bennett stood in the music room. Miss Ruiz played a song on the piano. The other kids clapped their hands. Bennett did not clap. His hands felt shy, like they wanted to hide in his pockets.

Then Miss Ruiz played "Twinkle, Twinkle." She pointed at the big yellow drum. She tapped it once. Boom. She tapped it again. Boom. Bennett watched her hand go up and down. When her hand went down, the drum made a sound. He tried clapping when her hand went down too. Clap. Clap. Clap.

Miss Ruiz poured tiny cups of milk for singing well. Bennett drank his and smiled. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star," he sang, all by himself. Miss Ruiz clapped for him. "Again," said Bennett.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Oliver sat at the dinner table. He had a plate of brown beans. He wanted to count them all by himself.

"One, two, three," said Oliver. He touched a bean with each word. His spoon slipped. The beans rolled away! "Oh no," said Oliver. "Where did my numbers go?"

Mama smiled. "Let's fetch a spoon that stays still." She gave him a big spoon. Oliver tried again. He tapped each bean slowly. "One, two, three, four, five." The beans stayed on the plate. Tapping made counting easy.

"Dada, count with me?" asked Oliver. Dada held up his fingers. They counted together. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten beans, all in a row.

Oliver clapped his hands. "I did it! Ten beans!" Then he picked one up and ate it. "Now nine," said Oliver, laughing.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Evan wanted a backyard picnic. But his things were all mixed up in one big box. He dumped them out on the grass.

"Let's make piles," said Mom. Evan picked up a toy car. It was his favorite toy. "Toys!" he said. He put the car, a ball and a duck that could ride on wheels into the toy pile. One, two, three toys.

Then he held up an apple. "Food!" he said. He put the apple, a banana and bread into the food pile. One, two, three foods. Then he heard a soft sound. A ladybug crawled on his shoe. "Animal," said Evan. A bird flew down too. One ladybug, one bird.

Then the dog ran by and grabbed the bread. "No, that is food for us!" said Evan. Mom gave the dog a bone instead. The dog chewed it happily.

Evan carried his toy pile to the little desk by the fence. He set his picnic on top. He ate his apple and played with the car.

Mom sat with him under the tree. The ladybug landed on the bread. Evan laughed.

"Hello, little picnic friend," he said.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Isabelle went to the farm with Grandpa. A little goat stood by the fence. "Hello, goat," said Isabelle. The goat looked at her. Isabelle looked back. "I see you with my eyes," she said. Grandpa smiled.

Next they walked to the hen house. The hens were noisy. "Cluck, cluck, cluck!" Isabelle covered her ears. "I hear the hens with my ears," she said. Then she touched a soft white feather on the ground. "I touch it with my hands," she said.

Grandpa had a gift for Isabelle. It was a shiny red apple. Isabelle held it. She sniffed it. "I smell it with my nose," she said. Then she took a big bite. "Yum! I taste it with my mouth."

Then Isabelle smelled something new. It was warm and sweet. Her nose led her to the farm kitchen. Farmer Beth was there. She was going to bake bread. "Would you like to watch?" asked Beth. Isabelle stood far back and watched. Beth put the bread in the oven.

At last the bread was ready. Beth cut a small piece for Isabelle. Isabelle sniffed it, tasted it, and hugged Beth. "My nose found it!" she said. Beth laughed and gave the goat a crust too.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Josephine wanted warm milk for snack time. The milk was cold from the fridge. "Brrr," said Josephine. "Too cold."

Miss Ada took the small pot. She set it on the stove. A little fire clicked on under it. Josephine stood back and watched. "The fire is hot," said Miss Ada. "Only I touch the pot."

Josephine waited. She waited slowly. Then steam came up. Little bubbles went fast, fast, fast. The milk got warm. Miss Ada poured it into Josephine's big cup.

Josephine took a sip. "Warm now!" she said. She gave the cup a kiss. "Thank you, milk."

Tommy slid fast across the floor. Josephine walked slow, slow, slow, so her cup would not spill. She sat down by the big window. Outside, a big dog ran fast. A small bird sat still.

Josephine held her warm cup with both hands. "Miss Ada," she said, "the cold milk went in. The warm milk came out."

Miss Ada smiled. "Yes it did," she said.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Alexis sat at the table for dinner. Mom set down a basket of warm rolls. His big sister took one roll. Alexis wanted one too. He grabbed for the basket. The basket was heavy. It tipped, and a roll rolled off the table. Dad picked up the roll. "Let's try again," Dad said. Alexis waited. His sister passed the basket to him. He took one roll with his hand. The roll was soft and warm.

Mom smiled. "You waited for your turn," she said. Alexis chewed his roll. He thought about school. Ben had the red truck today. Alexis had wanted it. He had grabbed, and Ben had cried. Then Ben gave him the truck. Alexis had given it back.

After dinner, Alexis washed his hands at the sink. The water was warm. Mom held the towel for him. "Tomorrow I will wait," Alexis said. He put his teddy bear in his bag. "Ben can hold him first." Mom kissed his ear. Alexis smiled and zipped the bag shut.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Jacob stood in the bathroom. He wanted to find his red toothbrush.

He used his eyes to look. He saw a cup by the sink. No toothbrush there.

Then he used his ears. He heard a drip, drip, drip. The faucet was leaking. "Mom, the sink is talking," he said.

Mom smiled. She came in and turned the tap. The drip stopped. "There," she said. "All quiet now."

Jacob sniffed with his nose. The towel smelled like soap. He touched it with his hands. It was soft and warm from the dryer, like a furry little cat.

He looked down at a small rug. He stepped on it with his toes. The rug was fuzzy too.

Then he saw something red. It was behind the soap. "My toothbrush!" he said. He did not miss it anymore.

Mom put a dot of toothpaste on it. It tasted like strawberries. Jacob brushed his teeth.

"Nice and clean," said Mom. Jacob grinned at the mirror.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Ivy wanted to draw a cat. But the paper box at the library was empty. "Oh no," said Ivy.

The librarian, Miss Ana, held up a new tablet. "Want to try this?" she asked. "Yes, please!" said Ivy. Miss Ana pressed the little button on top. The screen woke up. It was bright, like morning.

"Now you try," said Miss Ana. Ivy pressed the button. Tap. The screen went dark. She pressed it again. Tap. The screen woke up again. Ivy laughed. "I made it sleep! I made it wake!"

She tapped the green squiggle. The drawing app opened. Ivy drew a big orange cat with three eyes. "Silly cat," she said.

Then it was time to go. Ivy pressed the button. Tap. The screen went to sleep. She put the tablet in the basket, just like Miss Ana showed her.

"I will remember this in summer," said Ivy. "My cat can wake up too!"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
The big game was on TV today. Jaxon marched into the living room with his red flag. Everyone was there. Dad, Gran, and Uncle Theo. Even the neighbor, Mr. Bell.

"Where is the remote?" said Dad. It was lost. No remote, no game. Everyone looked under the couch. Gran looked behind the chair. Jaxon looked by the toy box. Then he had an idea. He pushed the big button on the TV himself. The screen lit up. The crowd on TV roared. Everyone in the room roared too.

The game began. Uncle Theo's team ran fast. Then they got slow, slow like a turtle. "Come on!" Jaxon shouted. He waved his flag high. Dad jumped up. Gran clapped. Jaxon clapped too, and Mr. Bell's little dog barked and barked.

The team kicked the ball. It went in the net. "Goal!" everyone yelled. The dog spun in a circle. Jaxon waved his flag so fast it made a whoosh sound. Uncle Theo lifted him way up high. "We win!" said Jaxon, and the room was full of happy, noisy people.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Ezra went to the farmers' market with Mama. A kind lady gave out warm toast. "Can I put butter on it?" Ezra asked. "Yes, you can," said the lady.

The lady gave him a small knife with a smooth, flat edge. She put a little butter on the tip. Ezra spread it slowly. The butter made the toast shine. "I did it!" he said. "Slow hands, slow hands," said Mama.

Next to the toast stood a jug of juice and a small cup. Ezra wanted milk instead. The lady found a tiny milk carton. "What if I pour too fast?" Ezra asked. "Then we wipe it up," said Mama. Ezra poured slowly. Not one drop spilled. The cup filled up. "Slow hands," whispered Ezra, and he drank his milk all gone.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Leah went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about a dog. Where could it be?

The library had big shelves. Shelf one had books with animals. Leah saw cats, birds and one big bear. She patted the bear on the cover. "Not a dog," she said.

Shelf two had books about toys. There were balls, blocks and drums. No dogs there. Shelf three had books about foods. Apples, bread and eggs smiled at her. Still no dog.

Then Leah saw a fluffy tail stick out of a bag. A real puppy! Its wet nose touched her hand. The puppy sniffed the food shelf and sat down by the animal shelf instead. "You like your own shelf!" Leah said. The librarian laughed. "Can we take him home for a visit?" Leah asked her dad. "Can we, can we?"

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Sienna sat at the craft table at camp. She wanted to make a butterfly. She had paper, glue, and sparkly paint.

Sienna poured the glue. Then she poured some more. Then some more. "Ooh, too much glue!" said her friend Milo. The glue made a big puddle. Sienna put her paper butterfly on the puddle. She pressed it down.

When she lifted it up, the butterfly stuck to her hand! "Come back, butterfly!" said Milo. They laughed. It flapped on her fingers like a real butterfly. "Silly glue," said Sienna. The teacher, Miss Jo, came to help. "Wet glue makes things stick," said Miss Jo. "We need it to dry." She gave them paper towels. Sienna wiped her dirty, sticky hands.

Then Miss Jo showed them a trick. She put the wet paintings in a bag. She hung the bag in the sun by the window. "Now we wait," she said. The children watched. Soon the glue turned clear and not sticky. Sienna peeled her butterfly off the table. It came off in one whole piece. "It can fly now," she said. She held it up and made it flap. "Look at my butterfly go!"

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Jasper wanted to feed his toy bunny. But the bunny had no carrots. "That is a problem," said Jasper.

He looked in the toy box. He found a ball and a truck and a drum. Those were toys. A bunny could not eat toys.

He looked in the fridge with Dad. He found milk, cheese and apples. Apples were food. But bunnies like carrots best.

Then Jasper saw a big orange thing. "Guess what that is," said Dad. "A carrot!" said Jasper. Dad washed it and cut it with a safe knife.

Jasper was gentle. He set the carrot by the bunny. Then the real bunny hopped over from her cage. Nibble, nibble, nibble.

"She likes it," said Jasper. He patted her soft ears. "More carrots tomorrow," he whispered to her. The bunny's nose went wiggle, wiggle, wiggle.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Lea sat at the big art table. She wanted to paint a green frog. But there was no green paint. "Oh no," said Lea. "My frog needs green."

Miss Mia smiled. "Look at the cups," she said. "One cup has yellow paint. One cup has blue paint." Lea counted them. "One cup, two cups," she said. She dipped her brush in the yellow. She made one dot on the paper. Then she dipped in the blue. She made one dot on top. "One dot, two dots," said Lea.

The dots touched. They mixed. The yellow and blue made green! Lea clapped her hands. "Green!" she said. Now she could paint her frog.

Next to her, a baby in a stroller watched. The baby kicked and cooed. Lea painted one green leg, two green legs, three green spots. She painted until her whole frog was full of green. Miss Mia held the paper up high to dry, near the window where the sun could warm it, like a little oven that cooks bread. "All done," said Miss Mia. Lea waved her green frog at the baby. "Ribbit!" said Lea.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Ellie sat at the big table. Grandma put down a bowl of rice. Uncle Ben put down bread. Everyone had a plate, but nobody ate.

"Wait," said Grandpa. "We say our words first."

Ellie wanted the bread now. She reached for it. Mama held her hand gently. "First the words," said Mama.

Grandpa held out his hands. Grandma took one hand. Uncle Ben took the other. Soon everyone at the table was holding hands. Ellie's hand went in Mama's hand. Then her other hand went in Grandpa's big hand. The circle went all the way around the table.

Grandpa said the blessing. His voice was slow. "Thank you for this food. Thank you for family." Everyone said, "Amen."

Ellie looked at her hands. When she held hands, the circle happened. The circle made everyone wait. Then everyone ate together.

"Now Ellie," said Grandpa. "You try."

Ellie took a big breath. "Thank you," she said. "For rice. And bread. And everybody."

"Amen," said everyone, even little Cousin Sam.

Then Grandpa picked up his fork. And Ellie finally got her bread.

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Sofia climbed into the car. She held her favorite toy rabbit tight. "We are going to the dentist!" said Mama. "He will look at your teeth."

Sofia was excited. Then she thought of something. "My tooth feels funny," she said. She wiggled it with her finger. It moved! "Mama, my tooth wiggles!" Mama smiled in the mirror. "That means it is getting loose," she said. "A new tooth will grow in its place."

At the dentist, the chair went up and up. The dentist looked in Sofia's mouth. "I see a loose tooth!" he said. He gave her a small mirror. Sofia looked inside. She could see all her little teeth, white as pearls. "There it is!" she said. She waved the mirror at her rabbit. "Look, one tooth is going on a trip!"

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Rehmat wanted to build a big tower. She found small blocks first. The small blocks made a small tower. Too small! She looked for big blocks.

She found two big blocks under the table. The big blocks made a big tower. Rehmat clapped her hands.

Then her brother ran in, fast. He bumped the tower. Down it fell. "Oh no," said Rehmat. She felt grumpy. Her face went hot and red.

Mama came in. "Slow down," Mama said to Rehmat. Rehmat breathed slowly. She pointed at the fallen blocks. "Big fall," she said. Mama smiled. "Build it again," she said.

Rehmat picked up one block. Then one more. The tower grew big again. She put a small letter block on the very top. "All done!" said Rehmat.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Parker was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make blueberry pancakes for his family. Grandma said he could help. He got a big bowl and a wooden spoon.

First, Parker poured in the mix. Then he cracked an egg into a small nest of paper towels. The batter looked lumpy. "It is bumpy," said Parker. "Keep stirring," said Grandma. Parker stirred and stirred. He peeked into the bowl. The lumps were getting small. He stirred some more. Now the batter was smooth like a river. His stirring had made the lumps go away!

Grandma put the pan on the stove. That part was for grown-ups, so Parker watched from his chair. Grandma poured the batter, and Parker dropped in blueberries. "They look like little blue boats," he said. The pancakes rose up big and round.

Soon Mom and Pop came to the table. Parker gave everyone two pancakes. He even gave Grandma the biggest one. Mom took a bite. "These are the best pancakes ever," she said. "Who made them?" Parker smiled big. "Me and Grandma. And my spoon!" After breakfast, Parker let his toy bunny ride on the empty bowl like a sled. "More pancakes tomorrow," he said.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Weston wanted to play house in the backyard. He set his bear on a square rug by the door. "You are my baby," Weston told him. But the bear kept tipping over. He would not sit up.

Weston tried again and again. The bear flopped to the side each time. Weston felt sorry for him. "Don't worry, baby," he said. Then he had an idea. He stuffed a small blanket behind the bear. The blanket held the bear up. The bear sat tall and still. "There," said Weston. "Now you can watch me cook."

Weston stirred a pot of pretend soup. He used a stick and dry leaves. "Soup is ready," he called. Dad came over and sniffed the pot. "Yum," said Dad. "May I have some?" Weston poured the pretend soup into a cup. Dad drank it all up and smiled. Weston gave the bear a pat on his soft head.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Nova went to the big hall with her grandma. Long wooden tables stood in rows. Everyone was bringing pots and bowls. The food smelled warm and good.

Nova wanted to start eating the bread right away. Grandma held her hand. "First we say our blessing," Grandma said. "You can help this time." Grandma showed Nova how to fold her hands. Nova tried it. Her fingers slipped apart. She folded them again. This time they stayed. Grandma said the blessing, and Nova said the last word with her. When they finished, everyone smiled and picked up their forks.

Then Uncle Ben clapped his hands. "Wait!" he said. He ran to the door. A late guest stood there with a big present in her arms. "We say it again so she can hear it too," said Grandma. Nova folded her hands and said the last word loudly. The new lady heard her all the way across the wooden table.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
It was Everett's birthday at Grandma's house. Everyone came in cars. They came from their own homes far away. Everett wanted to blow out his candles. But first the cake had to come out.

Grandma put the candles in the cake. Then Grandpa lit them with a match. Grandpa lit one candle. That candle lit the next candle. Then that one lit another. Soon all four candles glowed. "Look, Everett," said Grandma. "The fire walks from one to the next."

Everett watched the little flames. He waited a long time. Then everyone sang the birthday song. They sang slowly and loudly.

"Make a wish," said Grandma. Everett took a big breath. He blew and blew. All the candles went dark. Smoke curled up like a little ribbon. Everyone clapped and cheered. "Happy birthday, Everett!" they said. Everett smiled big. Then he asked, "Can we do the candles again?"

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Elijah wanted to find the tiny toy horse at school. He had seen it once, under the toy shelf. He could not reach it.

Miss Ada knelt down beside him. "Let's count the blocks while we look," she said. She put ten blocks in a row. "One, two, three." Elijah touched each block with his finger. "Four, five, six," he said. The blocks made a soft tapping sound.

Then Elijah saw it. When his finger tapped block seven, the horse moved. It slid out from under the shelf. "It wiggled!" said Elijah. Miss Ada smiled. "Your tap made it move," she said.

Elijah tapped block eight, then nine. The horse slid out more. He tapped ten. The tiny horse sat right by his shoe. Elijah picked it up. It was smooth and warm. He held it to his ear. "Go, horsey," he said softly. Then he trotted it up Miss Ada's arm, all the way to her shoulder.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Bennett was at Grandma's house. He wanted to help cook lunch for the whole family. Grandma said, "You can make the butter." Bennett blinked. Butter came from the store, in a box. How could a kid make butter?

Grandma poured cold cream into a jar. She screwed the lid on tight. "Shake it," she said. "Shake it hard." Bennett shook the jar. He shook it up high. He shook it down low. He shook it so fast his arms felt dizzy and tired.

Then something changed inside the jar. The sloshy sound went away. There was no more swish, swish. Bennett looked in. A soft yellow lump sat in the jar. Little white liquid floated around it. The cream had turned into butter! It happened because he shook it and shook it.

Grandma washed the yellow lump in cold water. She spread it on warm bread. Bennett carried the plate to the table, one slow step at a time. Mom took a bite. Dad took a bite. Even the baby waved her hands.

"This is the best butter ever," said Dad. Bennett sat up tall and looked at his empty jar. "Tomorrow," he said, "I will shake two jars."

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Audrey went to the pharmacy with Mama. Today was a big day. Audrey would get a shot.

"I want to be brave," said Audrey. She held Mama's hand tight.

The nurse came with a little bandage. On it was a tiny cat. "You get a cat bandage after your shot," said the nurse.

Audrey looked at the cat bandage. Then she looked at the nurse. "If I get the shot, I get the cat?" she asked.

"Yes," said the nurse. "First the shot, then the cat."

Audrey sat very still. The nurse cleaned her arm with a cool, wet cotton ball. Then came the shot. It was quick, like a tiny pinch.

"Done!" said the nurse. She pressed the cotton ball down. Then she peeled open the bandage. She stuck the little cat on Audrey's arm.

Audrey looked down. The cat sat on her arm. She had gotten the shot, and now she had the cat.

"Look, Mama!" said Audrey. She waved her arm in the air.

At the desk, the pharmacist poured a cup of water for Mama. Audrey drank a deep, happy sip too.

On the way home, Audrey showed everyone her arm. "I got a shot," she said. "And the shot gave me a cat."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Peyton sat at Grandma's big table. She wanted to make a picture for Grandpa. Grandma gave her paper and glue. Peyton squeezed the glue. It made a fat, shiny line. Then she opened the glitter jar.

But the glitter jar was empty. Peyton looked all around the room. She fished in the art box for more glitter. Her hand came out with soft paper dots instead.

Peyton pushed a paper dot onto the wet glue. It stuck! The glue was still wet, so the dots stayed. She pushed on more dots. Red, blue, and yellow. The dots made a bright flower.

Grandma brought a fresh apple for a snack. Peyton kept working. Grandpa came in and saw the picture. "A flower for me?" he said.

"Yes," said Peyton. "It sticks."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Jaxson sat at the dinner table. He banged his spoon on his cup. "Supper smells good!" he said. He felt excited.

Then Daddy set down a big bowl of pasta. Jaxson smiled a big smile. "Yum!" he said. He was happy.

But then his fork slipped. Splat! His pasta fell on the floor. Jaxson's face went sad. His chin wobbled. "My pasta," he said.

Molly the dog ran in fast. She gobbled the pasta up. Jaxson felt angry. He made a grumpy face. "Bad dog!" he said.

Then Molly licked his toe under the table. It tickled! Jaxson laughed. Hmm, he thought. First I was sad. Then I was mad. Now I laugh?

Thunder boomed outside. Boom! Jaxson jumped. He felt scared. He held Mama's hand tight.

Mama put new pasta on his plate. "Eat up," she said. Jaxson ate it all. His sister made her doll dance on the table. Jaxson giggled and clapped.

Molly wagged her tail. Jaxson waved his spoon and sang, "Happy again, happy again!"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Rowan went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. Today was the lantern festival. Rowan wanted to hang his lantern on the long string. But the string was too high for him.

First, the lanterns stayed dark. The hall felt dim and gray. Rowan held his lantern in his hands.

Then a grown-up lit one lantern. Warm light spilled out of it. The light made the wall glow. Rowan saw the paper turn bright.

"Papa, my lantern too?" asked Rowan.

Papa took the lantern and held it near the grown-up. A little flame woke up inside. Rowan's lantern grew bright and warm.

Now came the hanging. Papa lifted Rowan up, up, up. Rowan reached out. He hooked his lantern on the string. It swayed next to all the other lights.

Then something surprised Rowan. His lantern was shaped like a bunny. Its ears made two shadows on the wall. The shadows looked like a big soft rabbit hopping.

"Look, Mama! My bunny is dancing!"

Mama held his hand. The hall was full of glowing light. Rowan smiled at his bunny dancing on the wall.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Audrey stood by the letter wall in the school library. She wanted to find the letter for her own name. There were so many letters. She did not know where to start.

Mrs. Bell pointed at a big red letter. "This one is A," she said. "It says a, a, a." Audrey looked at the A. Then she looked at the apple picture below it. She said, "A, a, apple!" Mrs. Bell smiled and nodded.

Audrey ran her arm along the wall. She stopped at B. "B says b, b," she said. The picture below was a bee. It went bzz, bzz, bzz. Audrey laughed. She found A again. She put it and B together on the little table. "A, B," she read out loud. "That is how my name starts!" She gave the letter A a big hug, and Mrs. Bell clapped.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Sadie ran to the swings with her grandma. "Stay where I can see you," said Grandma. Sadie nodded. She pumped her legs. The swing went up and down.

Then Sadie saw the big slide. It was far away. She wanted to go there all by herself. She let go of the swing. She started to run. "Sadie, wait," called Grandma. Sadie stopped. Grandma took her hand. They walked together. That was better. Grandma's hand was warm.

Near the slide, a man was cooking at a little grill. It made sizzling sounds. Smoke went up, up, up. Sadie could feel heat on her face, even from far away. "That part is hot," said Grandma. "We stay back here." Sadie touched the cold metal pole of the slide. Cold felt nice. Hot did not. She kept her hands on the cold pole only.

Sadie saw something shiny on the ground. It was a short, pointy stick of metal. She reached for it. Grandma held her hand back right away. "Not that one," said Grandma. Grandma picked it up with a napkin and put it in the trash. Then it was Sadie's turn. She climbed the steps. She sat down. Whoosh! Down she went, fast, into the soft sand. "Again!" said Sadie. Grandma laughed and held out her hand.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Aubrey sat at the little table in the computer lab. She wanted to draw a cat. But the tablet was dark. She pressed the screen. Nothing happened. She pressed it again. Nothing.

"Try the round button," said her teacher. "The one on the side."

Aubrey found the round button. She held it and counted, "One, two, three." The screen woke up. It was bright now. Her round button made the light come.

On the screen she saw little squares. She looked and looked. "That one," she said, pointing to a square with a paintbrush. She tapped it. The drawing app opened. There was a white page just for her.

She picked green. She picked pink. She mixed the two colors on her page. Now she had a new greeny-pink cat with long whiskers.

Then it was time to go. Aubrey pressed the round button again, counted, "One, two, three," and the screen went dark. She put the tablet on the shelf, all by herself.

"Look at my cat," she said to her teacher. "I made it before the light went to sleep."

Her teacher smiled. "You put it away all by yourself, too."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Alexander wanted to help make lunch. The kitchen was warm and sunny. He stood next to Mama at the big counter.

Mama put a pot on the stove. Alexander saw the pot make steam. The steam went up, up, up. "Steam is hot," said Mama. She held his hand near, but not close. Alexander pulled his hand back fast. Hot meant no touch.

So Alexander helped in his own way. He put bread on a plate. He drew a picture with his pencil for the menu. It was a big red pot with steam. Mama clapped. "Our best menu ever," she said.

Then the toaster went pop. Out jumped a toast, high in the air. It landed right on Alexander's picture. Alexander laughed and laughed. "Toast wants lunch too," he said. Mama smiled and took the hot toast out with her big glove. She gave Alexander the plate. "You carry the cold plate," she said. "I carry the hot things." Alexander walked slowly, holding it with two hands. He did not drop one crumb.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Josephine ran to the library shelf. She wanted the counting book with the red cover. But it was too high up!

"Let's ask the singing corner," said the librarian. "Our story time is starting." Josephine sat down fast.

The librarian sang, "One, two, three, four, five." The children clapped along. Then she sang, "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Josephine clapped ten times.

After the song, the librarian stood up. "Singing made us hungry for books. Let's pick some!" Josephine followed her to the shelf.

"Now you can reach," said the librarian. She knelt down and pointed. The red book was on the low shelf, sitting straight in a row. Josephine pulled it out. She looked at all ten ducks on the cover.

"Ten little ducks," she read. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

The librarian laughed. "You found it all by yourself."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Julia went to the band room with her class. Mr. Bell showed the drums. He showed the bells. Then he showed a big drum with a soft stick. "This one is for you," he said. "Its name is Boomer."

Julia tapped Boomer very softly. Boomer made a small sound. Tap. It was tiny, like a mouse.

Julia wanted Boomer to be big. She tapped harder. Boom! The sound filled the room. The paper on the wall moved. The bells on the shelf shook a little. A boy named Sam covered his ears. He looked upset.

Julia put down her stick. She went to Sam. "Sorry it was too loud," she said. She gave him a hug. Sam smiled.

Then Julia tapped again. She tapped soft, soft, medium, medium. Sam clapped to the beat. Mr. Bell clapped too.

Julia held up her stick. "Watch this," she said. "Soft mouse, big bear!" Tap, tap, BOOM.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Evan ran up the porch steps at Grandma's house. "Grandma, I want a cookie!" he called. Grandma was shy of her cookies before lunch. "First, let's play a letter game," she said.

Grandma held up a card with a big B. Evan did not know it. Then Benny the cat jumped on the table. His tail was like a soft feather. "Benny," said Evan. "B! Benny starts with B!"

"Now you can have your cookie," said Grandma. She put it on a plate. "C is for cookie," said Evan. He bit it, and crumbs fell down. The crumbs made little dots on the table. "Look, Grandma! Dots! D for dots!" Grandma laughed. "You see letters everywhere!" Evan held up his cookie. "C is for cookie, C is for cookie!" he sang.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Matthew ran up the steps of the bookmobile. It was a little bus full of books. His mom held his hand.

"I want a book about trucks," said Matthew.

The library lady smiled. "First you need a card," she said. She wrote Matthew's name on a small card. It had a loose corner that wiggled. Matthew held it tight.

He found a truck book with a big red truck on the cover. He wanted to keep it forever.

"Can I keep it?" he asked.

"You can take it home," said the library lady. "But you bring it back. Then other kids can read it too."

Matthew frowned. He hugged the book to his chest.

"How will I know when?" asked Matthew.

"I will put this paper in the book," said the library lady. "When the day comes, the book goes back."

At home, Matthew read the truck book three times. He made truck sounds. "Beep, beep!"

On the way back to the bookmobile, Matthew sang a truck song. He gave the book to the library lady.

Then she showed him a shelf. "Look," she said. "A new truck book came today."

Matthew's eyes got big. "A new one?"

He took the new book home with his card. "Beep, beep," he said, waving from the steps.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Henry ran to the block corner. It was his first day of school. He wanted to build a big, big tower.

"Can I touch the tall part?" he asked his teacher.

"Build it first," she said with a smile.

Henry stacked one block. Then two. Then ten! The tower grew taller than his head.

Then he found a fat red block. It was very heavy. He put it on the very top.

The tower wobbled. The tower leaned. Down it came! Blocks went crash, boom, plunk all over the rug.

"Oh no," said Henry. "Why did it fall down?"

He looked at the fat red block. It was heavy at the top. He had an idea.

He put the heavy block at the bottom this time. Then he stacked the little blocks on top. The tower stood tall. It did not fall.

"Look, teacher! It stays up!"

A girl named Mia ran over. "Is that a tower or a doctor house?"

"It is a doctor tower," said Henry. "You can be the doctor."

Mia picked up a toy stethoscope. She touched the tower gently. "Beep beep," she said. "Your tower is healthy!"

Henry laughed and added one more small block on top.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Myles sat at the big art table. The sun came in the window. It was a sunny day. Myles wanted to paint a boat. But his boat looked wrong. It was just a blue smudge.

"My boat won't look like a boat," said Myles.

His teacher put a box on the table. Inside were sponges. A round sponge. A square sponge. A triangle sponge. A long rectangle sponge.

Myles dipped the square sponge in paint. He pressed it on the paper. A square appeared. It looked like a boat's body. Then he dipped the triangle sponge. He pressed it on top of the square. A triangle sail stood up.

"It's a boat!" said Myles.

He pressed the round sponge two times. Two circles made wheels for a truck. He pressed the rectangle sponge. It made a long road under the truck.

Maya leaned over. "Make a boat for me," she said.

Myles dipped the square again. He pressed it on her paper. Then the triangle went on top. Hop, hop, hop went his hand, stamp by stamp.

"Here is your boat," said Myles.

Maya held the paper up to the sunny window. The triangle sail was red. The square boat was blue. The paint dripped a little at the bottom, and Maya laughed.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. The dentist looked at her teeth. "All clean," he said. He gave her a sticker and a cookie.

Grace reached for the cookie. "Wait," said the nurse. "Where did your hands just go?"

Grace looked at her hands. They had touched the chair. They had touched her shoes. "I don't know," she said. "Germs can hide on hands," said the nurse. "Do you want to see something?"

The nurse took Grace to the sink. She put soap on Grace's hands. "Rub and count," she said. Grace rubbed and counted to twenty. Bubbles grew between her fingers.

Then the nurse held her hands under the light. "Look," she said. The hands shone. Grace dried them on a fuzzy towel and got a cup of ice water.

"Now can I have my cookie?" asked Grace. She ate it all up.
